sections.title: Tempo
sections.subtitle: Safe special delivery for important documents and time-sensitive items.

sections.title: About the project
sections.body:
Tempo is a safe special-delivery service built around documents and other time-sensitive items. It helps a customer request a trusted courier, confirm the sender and recipient, and follow the delivery from pickup to handoff.

The route model can also support food, pharmacy items, and custom errands, but the central product promise is document safety: the right item, handled by the right courier, delivered to the intended person.

I worked with the product team on the experience strategy, information architecture, core flows, interface design, and a reusable UI kit.

sections.title: One connected flow, a component library handed over, and one assumption still untested
sections.body:
The multi-stop route model reached a testable state. Category discovery, order building, route review, checkout and tracking exist as one connected flow, and the component library behind them was handed to the product team so new categories can be added without redesigning the order.

Tempo is still in progress. The route sheet has not yet been tested with customers who add several stops in a single session, and that behaviour is the assumption the whole product rests on.

Davit — replace this paragraph. This is the one thing the case study is missing and I cannot supply it: what actually happened. Did Tempo launch? How many screens went to build? What did the client do with the component library? If the project stalled, say so — a hiring manager trusts a named outcome more than a polished ending with none.

sections.title: Several errands often happen at the same time
sections.body:
A customer may order dinner while an important document waits across town. Standard delivery apps treat each request as a separate order, with another checkout, courier, fee, and tracking screen.

Tempo needed one flow that could combine different request types without making the route feel complex. Customers had to understand where the courier would go, how another stop affected the trip, and when the full order would arrive.

sections.title: One order, several stops, one courier
sections.body:
Customers add food, documents, pharmacy items, or a custom address to the same delivery. Tempo groups those stops, proposes an efficient order, and keeps the route visible before checkout.

The product explains the benefit in context. A time-saving message appears on the map, while the route sheet lists each stop and lets the customer adjust the plan before the courier starts.

sections.title: Delivery apps taught us conventions. Route planners taught us sequence.
sections.body:
We reviewed local delivery products to understand familiar patterns for browsing, checkout, and tracking. We also studied route-planning tools because Tempo’s core interaction depends on ordering several locations.

The comparison exposed a gap. Delivery apps handled products well but treated each order as a closed journey. Route planners handled stops well but lacked the shopping context customers expect. Tempo needed both mental models in one interface.

sections.title: The plus button turns one delivery into a route
sections.body:
A customer can add another pickup without leaving the active order. The new address joins the route sheet, and Tempo updates the map and estimated time.

Contextual guidance introduces the feature at the moment it becomes useful. Customers learn the route model through the task rather than a separate tutorial.

columns.title: The route explains each decision
columns.body:
The map shows the pickup order and highlights the proposed path. A compact message estimates the time saved through optimization.

The bottom sheet keeps delivery details close to the map. Customers can inspect stops, change their order, and start the delivery without losing spatial context.

sections.title: Wireframes made the new route model testable
sections.body:
We mapped the path from category discovery to order building, route review, checkout, and tracking. Low-fidelity screens helped us decide where customers could add a stop and how the route sheet should respond.

The wireframes also connected supporting journeys such as sign-in, profiles, order history, and delivery preferences.

sections.title: Categories organize a broad service without hiding the route
sections.body:
Tempo covers food, pharmacy items, alcohol, shops, documents, and custom deliveries. Categories and filters help customers enter through the need they recognize.

The route remains the shared layer across those categories. A customer can move between shopping and delivery planning while the current stops stay intact.

sections.title: A consistent experience across different requests
sections.body:
Restaurant cards, pharmacy listings, document delivery, and custom pickups use the same product language. Customers keep familiar controls as the content changes.

Small choices support the wider service. Delivery preferences can reduce waste, saved information speeds up repeat orders, and account history keeps past routes accessible.

sections.title: Sensitive deliveries need more than a tracking dot
sections.body:
Document delivery introduced a stronger trust requirement. Customers need confirmation that the courier received the correct item and delivered it to the intended recipient.

Tempo pairs delivery status with clear addresses, recipient details, and confirmation messages. Sign-in and recovery flows offer familiar paths through email or phone, so customers can return to an active order without confusion.

columns.title: Launching the service before the app
columns.body:
The business needed a public entry point while the mobile product remained in progress. We designed a landing page that explains Tempo’s promise, gives customers a phone number for delivery requests, and invites couriers and partners to join.

The page let the team begin learning from real demand before the full application was ready.

sections.title: The route is the product, not a final tracking screen
sections.body:
Tempo’s broad service catalog could have produced a collection of unrelated ordering flows. Treating the route as a persistent product layer gave those flows a shared structure, and it is the decision the rest of the design hangs on.

It is also the decision I would most want to see tested. When a customer adds a third stop, the fee changes and the arrival estimate moves — and I do not yet know whether that reads as the system working or as the price quietly going up. That is a trust question, not a visual one, and no amount of polish settles it.
